newsitem.title: UK: Britain admits error in Nazi gold report.
newsitem.headline: Britain admits error in Nazi gold report.

text.p: The British government admitted on Friday that it had wrongly accused Switzerland of turning over to Allied powers little more than a tenth of the Nazi gold it agreed was in Swiss bank vaults at the end of World War Two.
The admission by the Foreign Office of an error in a report it published last September was immediately welcomed by the Swiss Foreign Ministry, who praised its "intellectual honesty".

The original British report said that the director of the Swiss National Bank had let slip during post-war negotiations on the future of the gold -- much of it from Holocaust victims -- that Swiss banks held $500 million worth when the war ended.
A revised edition published by the Foreign Office on Friday corrected the figure to 500 million Swiss francs -- a major difference since in 1946, the dollar was worth 4.3 Swiss francs.
After the negotiations, Switzerland paid 250 million Swiss francs in connection with claims concerning Nazi gold, just under half the $130 million asked for by the Allied negotiators.

In a statement, the task force set up by the Swiss Foreign Ministry to look at the Nazi gold issue regretted "that Switzerland was hastily and flatly condemned in the international press on the basis of false facts".
It said Britain's honesty in admitting its error was an example to others who uncritically used individual documents to attack Switzerland on its role in the 1940s.

"Only careful, unprejudiced and comprehensive work can shed light on financial transactions more than 50 years old in which Swiss banks, trustees and other property administrators took part," it said.

Switzerland has convened a group of historians and other experts, who are expected to report in two or three years' time on a range of Swiss financial dealings during the war, including the gold purchases.

But World Jewish Congress president Edgar Bronfman and Senator Alfonse D'Amato, chairman of the U.S. Senate Banking Committee, called last month for the Swiss to make a gesture to compensate ageing Holocaust victims before the group reports.
